readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module walks through the three AWS storage types, block, object and file, and the main service behind each. It covers EC2 instance store and Amazon EBS with snapshots and Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, then Amazon S3 with its storage classes and lifecycle rules, then the managed file systems Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx. It ends with the hybrid and recovery services AWS Storage Gateway and AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, plus a real-life comparison of S3, EBS and EFS.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 6 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Storage: the three storage types, their AWS services and how shared responsibility shifts between fully managed, managed and unmanaged services.

Block Storage

  1. EC2 Instance Store and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS): fast but temporary instance store versus persistent EBS volumes.
  2. Amazon EBS Data Lifecycle: incremental EBS snapshots and automating them with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager.

Object Storage

  1. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3): objects, buckets, 11 nines durability and S3 access controls.
  2. Amazon S3 Storage Classes and S3 Lifecycle: every S3 storage class, what drives its price, and lifecycle rules that move or expire objects.
  3. Amazon S3 Demonstration: a console walk-through of buckets, uploads, metadata and a bucket policy.

File Storage

  1. Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS): the shared, self-scaling NFS file system, its classes, lifecycle and how it differs from EBS.
  2. Amazon FSx: managed Windows File Server, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS and Lustre file systems, and where FSx fits next to EFS and Storage Gateway.

Additional Storage Solutions

  1. AWS Storage Gateway: hybrid storage through S3 File Gateway, Volume Gateway and Tape Gateway, and how to pick one.
  2. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery: continuous server replication to AWS for fast recovery.

Cloud in Real Life

  1. Comparing Storage Services: three businesses matched to S3, EBS and EFS.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Block storage serves EC2, where instance store is very fast but loses data on stop or termination, while EBS volumes persist on their own inside one Availability Zone.
  • EBS snapshots are incremental, point-in-time backups kept in Amazon S3, and Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates their creation, retention and deletion.
  • Amazon S3 holds objects of up to 5 TB in globally named buckets, offers 11 nines of durability and keeps everything private by default.
  • S3 storage classes trade retrieval speed and resilience for price, from S3 Standard down to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
  • S3 Lifecycle rules move or delete objects as they age, while S3 Intelligent-Tiering shifts objects among its own access tiers automatically.
  • Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system that many instances share and that grows on its own, and its Standard classes replicate across Availability Zones.
  • Amazon FSx runs Windows File Server, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS and Lustre as managed services in the AWS Cloud.
  • AWS Storage Gateway links on-premises systems to AWS storage through file, volume and tape gateways, with local caching for hot data.
  • AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers continuously so they can be recovered in minutes.
  • Customer responsibility grows from fully managed services such as S3 and EFS, to managed EBS, to unmanaged instance store.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

The closing recap walks back through the module one storage type at a time. On the block side it sets short-lived instance store against durable EBS volumes, with snapshots and Data Lifecycle Manager handling automated protection. Amazon S3 stands for object storage and is framed as the base layer for much of what runs in the cloud. For files, EFS covers Linux workloads and FSx covers Windows, Lustre, OpenZFS and NetApp ONTAP, and Storage Gateway rounds things off as the link for hybrid designs. The recap does not return to S3 storage classes, S3 Lifecycle or AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, which the lessons above cover.

introduction-to-storage.html:
Introduction to Storage

Objectives

  • Tell block, object and apart.
  • Name the main AWS service for each type.
  • Apply the shared responsibility model to storage.

Notes

Why several storage types

  • Virtual AWS storage removes hardware from your and scales with demand.
  • The coffee shop keeps bean stock, sales, marketing material and secret recipes, each in a fitting container from jars to a safe, and data likewise needs matching storage.
  • Images and PDFs must come back whole, logs need fast, steady reads and writes, and shared manuals must reach every employee.
  • Databases, for constantly queried data, come in a later module.

Block storage

  • Data is split into blocks for fast access, and an edit rewrites only changed blocks, which suits frequently updated apps and databases.
  • Persistent, low-latency volumes attach to EC2 like drives and can be encrypted, snapshotted and modified in use without disruption.
  • Services: (unmanaged, temporary, high performance) and (managed, persistent).

Object storage

  • An object holds data, a unique ID and metadata, and any change rewrites the whole object.
  • Objects sit in flat buckets with practically unlimited room for unstructured data, and rich metadata helps search and analytics.
  • Best for rarely changing files such as videos, backups or logs.
  • Service: , fully managed, for any amount of data from anywhere.

File storage

  • A hierarchical file system shared over a network, needing little or no code change and growing without hardware to manage.
  • Fits shared-access apps such as content management systems.
  • Services: (fully managed ) and (fully managed Windows, Lustre and NetApp ONTAP file systems).

Other storage services

  • gives on-premises systems hybrid access to cloud storage.
  • recovers physical, virtual and cloud servers into AWS.

Shared responsibility for storage

  • Fully managed: AWS covers the whole stack, including durability, availability, and replication, and you handle data, access and configuration.
  • Managed: AWS keeps infrastructure, hardware redundancy and volume replication, and you plan backups, encryption, performance and capacity.
  • Unmanaged: AWS keeps only hardware and network running, and the data, durability included, is yours.

Visuals

  • Responsibility images: the customer's share grows from fully managed to managed to unmanaged.

Key takeaways

  • updates in pieces and serves EC2 through instance store and Amazon EBS.
  • keeps whole objects with metadata in flat Amazon S3 buckets.
  • File storage shares one file system through Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx.
  • Less AWS management means more customer responsibility.

Scenarios

  • Marketing images and PDFs that must come back whole point to object storage.
  • Manuals the whole shop opens point to file storage.

Terms

  • Block storage: storage that rewrites only the blocks that change.
  • Object storage: storage of self-contained objects (data, ID, metadata) in flat buckets.
  • File storage: a shared, hierarchical file system reached over a network.
  • Fully managed, managed, unmanaged: the three groups showing how much storage administration AWS takes on.

ec2-instance-store-and-amazon-elastic-bl.html:
EC2 Instance Store and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)

Objectives

  • Explain store, its benefits and when to use it.
  • Explain , its benefits and when to use it.

Notes

Block-level storage on EC2

  • keeps a file as bytes in disk blocks, so an update rewrites only the affected blocks.
  • That efficiency suits databases, enterprise software and file systems, like a laptop's hard drive.

Amazon EC2 instance store

  • Instance store is disk physically attached to the instance's host, not a stand-alone service, and is the default storage on some instance types.
  • Stopping or terminating the instance erases it, since a restarted instance usually lands on another host without that disk.
  • Being ephemeral, it suits data you can lose, such as buffers, caches and scratch space for heavy processing.
  • It serves one instance only and cannot be shared the way can.
  • Benefits: included with many instance types at no extra cost, with very low latency and high I/O because it sits on the host.

Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)

  • EBS volumes are virtual hard drives that attach to instances like external drives.
  • They live apart from the host on durable SSD or HDD media, so data survives stops, starts and terminations.
  • You choose size, type and configuration, provision the volume, attach it and let the application write to it.
  • A volume gives consistent low latency, attaches to one instance at a time, and can be backed up, resized and moved to another instance.
  • EBS replicates each volume automatically within its for availability and durability.
  • A volume lives in one Availability Zone, and so in one Region, and snapshots carry its data elsewhere.
  • Volume types differ in price and in performance, measured in (input/output operations per second) and tied to type and often size.
  • A volume never grows by itself, so you modify it to add capacity.
  • Back volumes up with incremental Amazon EBS snapshots.
  • Use cases: database hosting, application backups and quick development environments built from snapshots.

Benefits of detachable volumes

  • Migration and disaster recovery: snapshots copy data to other Availability Zones or Regions and restore it there.
  • changes: reattach a volume to a bigger or smaller instance and keep the data.
  • Cost and performance tuning: change type, size or IOPS on the fly without downtime.

Visuals

  • Instance store markers: a running instance holds data, the instance stops, and the data is gone, teaching non-persistence.
  • EBS markers: the same three steps with an end with the data intact, teaching persistence.

Key takeaways

  • Instance store does not persist, so a stop or termination erases it.
  • EBS persists, so an attached volume keeps its data through stops and terminations.
  • Instance store gives top I/O at no extra cost, but only for temporary data on one instance.
  • EBS volumes are sized and typed by you, sit in one Availability Zone and are protected by incremental snapshots.

Scenarios

  • Scratch space for heavy calculations fits instance store.
  • A database that must survive instance stops fits an EBS volume.
  • Moving to a larger instance type keeps the data by reattaching the EBS volume.
  • Knowledge checks practised instance store for fast temporary data and EBS for persistent, low-latency block storage.

Terms

  • Amazon EC2 instance store: temporary block storage on the instance's host, lost on stop or termination.
  • Amazon EBS: managed service providing persistent block storage volumes for EC2 instances.
  • EBS volume: a virtual hard drive in one Availability Zone that you attach to an instance.
  • IOPS: input/output operations per second, the performance measure for EBS volumes.
  • Ephemeral storage: storage whose data is lost when the instance stops or terminates.

amazon-elastic-block-store-amazon-ebs-da.html:
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Data Lifecycle

Objectives

  • Explain EBS snapshots and how they help manage data.
  • Explain the EBS data lifecycle and the service that automates it.
  • Identify what the customer owns for snapshots and .

Notes

EBS data lifecycle

  • Lifecycle management means creating, backing up and deleting volumes and snapshots to control cost and protect data.
  • Your data is your job under shared responsibility, so you provision, move, deprovision and back up volumes.

EBS snapshots

  • A snapshot is a , taken as often as needed, from daily to monthly.
  • Uses: disaster recovery, data migration, volume resizing and consistent production backups.
  • Monday's first snapshot copies everything and Tuesday's only the changes, so later ones are faster and much cheaper.
  • A snapshot can create many new volumes, each an exact copy of the source at that moment.
  • Snapshots sit in , redundantly across several Availability Zones.

How the snapshot chain works

  • The first snapshot is a full baseline of all blocks in use.
  • Later ones store only changed blocks and reference earlier ones, forming a chain for .
  • Each still acts as a full copy, AWS manages the links, and deleting one frees only data no other snapshot uses.

Duties and benefits

  • Your part: schedule snapshots, prune them to control cost, encrypt sensitive data, verify integrity and test restores.
  • Benefits: recovery from corruption, deletion or failure; cross-Region migration, resizing, cloning and cross-account sharing; and lower cost from storing only changes.

Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager

  • Snapshotting thousands of volumes by hand each week is slow and error-prone.
  • This uses policies to create, keep and delete snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs on a schedule.
  • It can run snapshots off-peak to limit performance impact, purge old backups and apply one policy organization-wide, which aids compliance.
  • It acts only on resources already in AWS.
  • Policy steps: create it (EC2 console, , , SDKs or ), target volumes or instances, optionally exclude root or data volumes, set schedules, then add extras.
  • Extras include cross-Region copies, cross-account sharing, tags, snapshot archiving and fast snapshot restore.

Visuals

  • Snapshot chain illustration: three markers go from a full baseline to linked incremental snapshots to safe deletion, teaching how incremental backups still act as complete copies.
  • Data Lifecycle Manager slides: the policy-building steps.

Key takeaways

  • Snapshots are point-in-time, incremental EBS backups kept in Amazon S3 across several Availability Zones.
  • Only the first snapshot is full, and deleting one never removes data another needs.
  • The customer schedules snapshots, controls their cost, encrypts them and tests restores.
  • Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates snapshot creation, retention and deletion through policies.

Scenarios

  • Restoring a volume after corruption starts from its latest snapshot.
  • Weekly manual snapshots across thousands of volumes give way to a Data Lifecycle Manager policy.
  • Knowledge checks practised snapshots for copying production into test environments and Data Lifecycle Manager for backups and cleanup at scale.

Terms

  • Amazon EBS snapshot: a point-in-time, incremental backup of an EBS volume stored in Amazon S3.
  • Point-in-time backup: a copy of data as it stood at one moment.
  • Incremental backup: a backup holding only what changed since the previous one.
  • Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager: fully managed service whose policies automatically create, keep and delete EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs.
  • Snapshot policy: a Data Lifecycle Manager rule set of targets, schedules and extra actions.

amazon-simple-storage-service-amazon-s3.html:
Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3)

Objectives

  • Explain , its benefits and its use cases.
  • Identify the S3 features for managing security.

Notes

What S3 is

  • A fully managed, highly available object store for virtually unlimited data, ideal for unstructured content like documents, images and video.
  • For the coffee shop, that means anything from receipts to staff training videos.
  • It integrates with other AWS services and serves cloud apps and on-premises workloads alike, from backups to data lakes.
  • Given permission, a bucket is reachable from anywhere, whatever its Region.

Objects and buckets

  • Every file is stored as an object, and objects go in buckets instead of directories, as a file sits in a folder on your drive.
  • An object has data, metadata and a key that names it uniquely in its bucket, plus properties such as a version ID and access control details.
  • Objects run from a few bytes to 5 TB per upload, and buckets have no size cap.
  • Each object is stored durably in multiple facilities, meaning several Availability Zones, within your chosen Region.
  • Bucket names are unique across AWS, and you set the name and Region at creation.
  • A bucket is the basic unit of access control, holds virtually unlimited objects and takes settings like versioning, logging and permissions.

Durability and versioning

  • For most storage classes AWS keeps redundant copies automatically, giving (99.999999999 percent) of durability, so losing an object within a year is vanishingly unlikely.
  • Versioning lets you bring back earlier versions after an accidental delete.

Benefits and uses

  • Storage scales with no fixed ceiling, and you pay only for what you store.
  • Lifecycle policies move objects between storage classes or expire them by your rules.
  • Uses: websites, content and media delivery, backups, archives, app data, data lakes and compliance retention.
  • An online store's product images on S3 survive a traffic spike with no scaling work, because AWS runs the service.

Security and privacy

  • Data starts private, reachable only by its creator until you grant access, though you may make buckets and objects public.
  • Bucket policies are resource-based, attach only to buckets and allow or deny actions on the bucket and all its objects.
  • Identity-based policies sit on users, groups or roles and set which buckets and objects they may use and how.
  • and in transit keeps stored objects and traffic confidential and helps meet security regulations.
  • Presigned URLs grant expiring access without touching the .
  • S3 Access Points simplify separate access rules for groups sharing one dataset.
  • S3 Audit Logs record every request, showing who accessed what and when.
  • Block Public Access, on the account or the bucket, overrides any bucket policy that would open data to the public.
  • Public access is thus set by these settings and policies, not by object tags or static website hosting.

Visuals

  • S3 elements timeline: two steps define objects (data, metadata, key) and buckets (globally named containers that group objects and carry policies).
  • Security tabs: three tabs cover bucket policies, identity-based policies and encryption, teaching the layers of S3 access control.

Key takeaways

  • S3 stores objects (data, metadata, key) in globally named buckets, up to 5 TB per object with no bucket limit.
  • Redundant copies give 11 nines of durability, and versioning undoes accidental deletes.
  • Everything starts private, and Block Public Access beats a permissive bucket policy.
  • Access is granted through bucket policies, identity-based policies, presigned URLs and Access Points.

Scenarios

  • Product images for an online store with traffic spikes fit S3's managed scaling.
  • Sharing a file briefly with an outside party fits a .
  • Several teams with different rights on one dataset fit S3 Access Points.
  • Knowledge checks practised S3 for mobile app media, troubleshooting blocked public access and S3 durability for video libraries.

Terms

  • Amazon S3: fully managed object storage for virtually unlimited data.
  • S3 object: the basic S3 storage unit of data, metadata and a key.
  • S3 bucket: a globally named container that holds objects and carries policies.
  • Object key: an object's unique name within its bucket.
  • Durability (11 nines): the 99.999999999 percent yearly odds that an S3 object stays intact.
  • S3 Versioning: keeping earlier object versions for restoring.
  • Bucket policy: a resource-based policy on a bucket and its objects.
  • Identity-based policy: a policy on a user, group or role that sets its S3 permissions.
  • Presigned URL: an expiring link granting temporary object access.
  • Amazon S3 Access Points: per-group access policies on a shared dataset.
  • Amazon S3 Audit Logs: logs of every request to S3 resources.
  • S3 Block Public Access: settings that block public access even when a policy allows it.

amazon-s3-storage-classes-and-s3-lifecyc.html:
Amazon S3 Storage Classes and S3 Lifecycle

Objectives

  • Describe each and how they differ.
  • Explain policies and how they affect cost.

Notes

Why storage classes exist

  • Each class balances performance, access, resiliency and cost, and some target data residency, unpredictable access or archiving.
  • One bucket can mix classes, chosen per object by access pattern.
  • Cost depends mainly on the class: per-GB storage rate, retrieval charges and (none for , 180 days for ).
  • The bucket's Region affects price too, though the class is a primary driver.

Frequent and changing access

  • S3 Standard: the general-purpose default when no class is named, with fast retrieval at an affordable price, for apps, games, dynamic websites, content distribution and big .
  • : for unknown or shifting access, S3 tracks use and moves each object to its cheapest suitable tier, with no lifecycle rules to manage.
    • The slide names three tiers (frequent, infrequent, archive instant access), while the video says four.
    • Good for data lakes and large datasets whose usage changes.

Infrequent access

  • : data used less often but needed fast, with S3 Standard's durability, throughput and latency, cheaper storage and a per-GiB retrieval fee, for backups and disaster recovery files.
  • : one instead of Standard-IA's three, so cheaper, for secondary backups or easily recreated data without needs.

Single-zone speed

  • : a single-zone class for the hottest, latency-sensitive data, answering consistently in single-digit milliseconds.
    • Versus S3 Standard, access is up to 10x faster and requests up to 80% cheaper.
  • Both one-zone classes cut cost or add speed but risk data loss if that zone is damaged.

Glacier archive classes

  • : rarely read archives returned in milliseconds, up to 68 percent cheaper than Standard-IA at equal speed, for things like medical images or media.
  • : cheaper archives read about once or twice a year, for backup, disaster recovery and offsite copies.
    • Expedited retrieval takes 1-5 minutes, and free bulk retrieval 5-12 hours.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive: the lowest-cost class, for data touched perhaps once or twice a year, with a default 12-hour retrieval.
    • Meant for long-term retention and digital preservation, such as compliance archives that finance, healthcare or government keep 7-10 years or more.

Amazon S3 Outposts

  • Brings S3 storage, APIs and features to an on-premises environment, for local data residency and for speed when data must stay near local apps.

S3 Lifecycle

  • Interest in data often fades, like a social media post that is busy for days and ignored months later.
  • Lifecycle configurations automate this for an object or group of objects with two kinds of action.
    • Transition actions move objects to another class at a set age, such as Standard-IA after 30 days or Glacier Deep Archive after a year.
    • Expiration actions delete objects for good, such as when compliance no longer needs them.
  • Transitions happen within the same bucket, with no manual copying between buckets.
  • Rules should follow the access curve, since archiving too early blocks quick access and expiring too early deletes needed data.
  • Typical candidates are periodic logs kept a week or a month, and documents that cool off, are archived for a set period, then deleted.
  • studies access patterns to show when a cheaper class pays off.

Visuals

  • Storage class slides: nine slides from S3 Standard to S3 Outposts, teaching which class fits which access pattern.
  • Lifecycle example diagram: an untouched object moves from S3 Standard to Standard-IA after 30 days, to Glacier Instant Retrieval after 60 more, and is deleted after 365 days there.

Key takeaways

  • S3 Standard is the default for frequently used data, and Standard-IA or One Zone-IA cost less for data used less.
  • Glacier classes are for archives: Instant Retrieval in milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval in minutes to hours, Deep Archive in about 12 hours at the lowest price.
  • Intelligent-Tiering moves objects among its own access tiers when usage is unknown or changing.
  • S3 Lifecycle transition and expiration actions move or delete objects as they age.
  • Price depends on the class's storage rate, retrieval fees and minimum storage duration.

Scenarios

  • Medical images opened rarely but needed instantly fit Glacier Instant Retrieval.
  • Regulatory archives kept for a decade fit Glacier Deep Archive.
  • Moving old data to Glacier after a year and deleting it when compliance ends is a lifecycle policy.
  • Knowledge checks practised matching lifecycle transitions to a fading access pattern and defining S3 Lifecycle.

Terms

  • S3 storage class: an S3 tier with its own performance, resiliency and price.
  • S3 Standard: the default general-purpose class.
  • S3 Intelligent-Tiering: a class that moves objects among its access tiers automatically.
  • S3 Standard-IA: a class for infrequently used data needing fast retrieval, with a retrieval fee.
  • S3 One Zone-IA: a cheaper infrequent-access class in one Availability Zone.
  • S3 Express One Zone: a single-zone class for the fastest, most frequent access.
  • S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: an archive class with millisecond retrieval.
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: an archive class with retrieval in minutes to hours.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive: the cheapest class, with retrieval in about 12 hours.
  • Amazon S3 Outposts: S3 storage delivered on premises through AWS Outposts.
  • Minimum storage duration: the shortest storage period a class commits you to.
  • S3 Lifecycle: rules that transition or expire objects automatically.
  • Transition action: a lifecycle rule that moves objects to another class.
  • Expiration action: a lifecycle rule that permanently deletes objects.
  • S3 Storage Class Analysis: a feature that analyzes access patterns to suggest class changes.

amazon-s3-demonstration.html:
Amazon S3 Demonstration

Objectives

  • Move around the .
  • Create and configure an .
  • Upload single files and whole folders.
  • Set system-defined and user-defined object metadata.

Notes

Creating a bucket

  • Search for S3 in the console and choose Create bucket.
  • No bucket in any AWS account may share the name, and the demo keeps the N. Virginia Region.
  • Block all public access starts on, keeping outsiders out, and stays on in the demo.

Folders and uploads

  • A folder adds structure to the empty bucket, with the default encryption accepted.
  • Upload, then Add files, puts single files in the folder.
  • Whole folders need drag and drop, the or an , and S3 preserves their hierarchy.

Object metadata

  • records basics such as creation date, size and storage class.
  • holds your own details, such as tags.

Bucket-level settings

  • Properties: versioning, tags, default encryption, Intelligent-Tiering archive configuration, static website hosting and more.
  • Permissions: Block Public Access, the , object ownership and cross-origin resource sharing (CORS).
  • Management: lifecycle, replication and inventory configurations.

Writing a bucket policy

  • Bucket policies are JSON documents controlling who may reach the objects inside.
  • The demo's policy lets another AWS account upload while the bucket owner keeps full control.
    • Effect: allow.
    • : the AWS account number allowed to upload.
    • Action: the call.
    • Resource: the parts of the bucket covered.
    • Condition: cross-account uploads succeed only when object ownership metadata is set correctly.

Object-level settings

  • The object URL works for anyone only when Block Public Access is off and bucket permissions allow it.
  • With Block Public Access on, the bucket policy decides exactly who gets in.
  • Object properties also include Object Lock, checksums, , the storage class, tags and metadata.
  • The Versions tab lists earlier versions to restore or delete.

Key takeaways

  • Bucket names are globally unique, and each bucket lives in a Region you choose.
  • New buckets block all public access by default.
  • Whole folders upload by drag and drop, the AWS CLI or an SDK, keeping their structure.
  • Object metadata is either system-defined or user-defined.
  • The demo's bucket policy is JSON with an effect, a principal, an action, a resource and a condition.

Scenarios

  • Letting another AWS account upload to your bucket uses a bucket policy whose condition protects owner control.
  • Recovering an overwritten or deleted file uses the Versions tab once versioning is on.

Terms

  • AWS Management Console: the web interface the demo uses to configure S3.
  • System-defined metadata: object details S3 records itself, such as size and storage class.
  • User-defined metadata: custom details you attach to an object, such as tags.
  • Principal: the account or identity a bucket policy statement applies to.
  • PutObject: the S3 API action that uploads an object.

amazon-elastic-file-system-amazon-efs.html:
Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS)

Objectives

  • Explain , its benefits and its use cases.
  • Explain EFS storage classes and their effect on price.
  • Explain EFS lifecycle policies and how they move data between classes.

Notes

What Amazon EFS is

  • Self-hosting a file system that many servers share, such as an analytics fleet on one dataset, means handling capacity, redundancy, backups and upkeep, whereas with EFS AWS scales and replicates it for you.
  • EFS is a fully managed, elastic file service on the Linux protocol, supporting POSIX-compliant Linux apps.
  • It grows to petabytes and shrinks as files change, without disrupting applications.
  • Thousands of concurrent NFS connections let many EC2 instances share files, and every change is visible to all of them at once, with no manual syncing.
  • Latency stays consistently low, with EFS Standard under a millisecond, though one instance's local instance store is usually faster.
  • Standard classes replicate across Availability Zones in a Region, so one zone failing does not cut access.

Static website on Amazon S3

notes.title: EC2 Instance Store and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)

lines: Instance store and Amazon EBS are both block storage, but only an EBS volume keeps its data when the instance stops.
Amazon S3 keeps each file whole as an object with its metadata, which suits photos, PDFs and videos that rarely change.
Amazon EFS shares a Linux NFS file system, while Amazon FSx runs Windows, Lustre and other file systems in the cloud.
Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx keep no cache on site, so shop systems that need fast local access, or that keep their backup routine, reach the cloud through AWS Storage Gateway.

notes.title: Amazon S3 Storage Classes and S3 Lifecycle

lines: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class to store in but returns data slowest and at the highest retrieval fee (lab values), so once the next read can wait a day it costs less over the year than S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
Archiving too early blocks quick access, since Deep Archive takes about 12 hours to return data that the owner needs within the hour.
A one-zone class costs less, but receipts sitting in it on the day its zone is damaged are lost, so it suits secondary backups or data that is easy to recreate.
An expiration action deletes objects for good, so it waits until compliance no longer needs the receipts.

goals.hint: Ask whether the disk sits on the instance's own host, since a stopped instance usually comes back on another host without that disk.

goals.label: At most 160 orders are lost with the zone
goals.hint: Everything in the failed zone goes with it, so ask which copy of the orders is kept outside the zone and how many hours of orders it misses.

goals.label: Snapshots cost at most 40 lab credits
goals.hint: Only the first backup copies everything and each later one stores just the changes, yet every extra one still adds to the bill.

notes.title: EC2 Instance Store and Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS)
Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) Data Lifecycle

lines: The stop erased the instance store, because that disk sits on the host the instance usually leaves, and no snapshot can protect it.
The Amazon EBS volume kept every order through the stop, since it lives apart from the host.
The volume lives in one Availability Zone and went with it, so only the orders since the last snapshot were lost, as snapshots sit in Amazon S3 across several zones.
Each snapshot after the full first one stores only the changes for 1 lab credit, so a shorter gap trades a bigger bill for fewer orders at risk.

questions.takeaway: Instance store data does not survive a stop, so anything kept there must be safe to lose and rebuild.

read.text: Stopping or terminating the instance erases it, since a restarted instance usually lands on another host without that disk.

questions.stem: The cafe keeps a menu image cache on an EC2 instance's instance store. To save money it stops the instance every night and starts it again each morning. Every morning the cache is empty and must be rebuilt. Which fact explains this?

options.text: EBS volumes keep their data through a stop and start.
options.why: This is true of EBS, but the cache sits on instance store, so it says nothing about the empty cache.

options.text: Snapshots can copy a volume's data to another Region.
options.why: This is true of EBS snapshots, but it describes backup and migration, not why the cache is gone.

options.text: Instance store gives very low latency and high I/O.
options.why: This is true of instance store, but speed does not explain why the cached images disappear overnight.

options.text: Instance store is erased when its instance is stopped.
options.why: Stopping the instance erases instance store, so the cache starts empty each morning.

questions.takeaway: After the first full snapshot, each EBS snapshot stores only the blocks changed since the one before.

read.text: The first snapshot is a full baseline of all blocks in use.

questions.stem: The cafe takes its first snapshot of the menu database volume on Monday and another on Tuesday. Why is Tuesday's snapshot faster and cheaper than Monday's?

options.text: It is kept in Amazon S3 across zones
options.why: Monday's snapshot is stored the same way, so where it sits cannot make Tuesday's cheaper.

options.text: It stores only the blocks that changed
options.why: Later snapshots save just the changed blocks and point back to earlier ones for the rest.

options.text: It can restore the whole volume alone
options.why: Acting as a full copy is true of every snapshot, so it does not explain the lower cost.

options.text: It can be copied to another Region
options.why: A cross-Region copy is an extra option for any snapshot and adds cost rather than saving it.

questions.takeaway: A database on one instance that must survive stops needs persistent, low-latency block storage from Amazon EBS.

read.text: They live apart from the host on durable SSD or HDD media, so data survives stops, starts and terminations.

questions.stem: The cafe runs its order database on one EC2 instance. It needs low-latency block storage for that instance whose data stays intact when the instance is stopped for maintenance. Which service fits?

options.text: Amazon EC2 instance store
options.why: Instance store is erased when the instance stops, so the order data would be lost.

options.text: Amazon EFS
options.why: EFS is a shared file system for many instances, not a block volume for one database server.

options.text: Amazon S3
options.why: S3 stores objects, not block storage that a database writes to like a disk.

options.text: Amazon EBS
options.why: An EBS volume gives one instance persistent, low-latency block storage that survives stops.

incidents.title: The S3 bill that keeps creeping up
incidents.brief: The cafe's Amazon S3 bill has grown every month this year. Menu photos, event pictures and daily order logs all sit in one bucket, and the owner wants the bill trimmed without losing anything staff still use.

steps.takeaway: S3 Storage Class Analysis studies how objects are read to show when moving them to a cheaper class pays off.

read.text: S3 Storage Class Analysis studies access patterns to show when a cheaper class pays off.

steps.stem: The cafe keeps menu photos, event pictures and daily order logs in one Amazon S3 bucket. Before moving any of them somewhere cheaper, the owner wants to see how often each group is actually read, so she knows where a move would pay off. What should she use to get this view?

options.text: S3 Storage Class Analysis
options.why: It watches how often each group of objects is read and shows where a cheaper class would save money, the view the owner wants before moving anything.

options.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
options.why: It moves objects among its own tiers by itself, but it gives the owner no report on each group to plan her own moves from.

options.text: S3 Lifecycle configuration
options.why: It moves or deletes objects on a schedule the owner sets, so it acts on a plan rather than showing her how often each group is read.

options.text: Amazon S3 Access Points
options.why: They give each group of users its own access policy on shared data, which says nothing about how often the photos or logs are read.

steps.takeaway: Rarely opened data that must still come back in milliseconds fits S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

read.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: rarely read archives returned in milliseconds, up to 68 percent cheaper than Standard-IA at equal speed, for things like medical images or media.

steps.stem: The cafe's old event photos are opened only a few times a year. When a customer asks to see one, though, staff must show it on the spot. Which storage class keeps these photos most cheaply while meeting that need?

options.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
options.why: It is built for rarely read archives that must still come back in milliseconds, at a low storage price.

options.text: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
options.why: Its retrievals take minutes to hours, so staff could not show a photo while the customer waits.

options.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
options.why: It is the cheapest class, but a retrieval takes about 12 hours by default, far too slow for this need.

options.text: S3 Standard
options.why: It suits data used often, so it costs more than needed for photos opened only a few times a year.

steps.takeaway: Lifecycle rules should follow how data is used, because an expiration that fires too early permanently deletes data still needed.

read.text: Expiration actions delete objects for good, such as when compliance no longer needs them.

steps.stem: A team member drafts an S3 Lifecycle rule that expires the daily order logs before the accountant has finished checking them. What goes wrong if the cafe applies this rule?

options.text: The logs are deleted for good and cannot be brought back
options.why: An expiration action removes objects permanently, so logs expired before the check ends are gone while the accountant still needs them.

options.text: The logs are archived where each read takes hours to finish
options.why: Slow archive reads follow a transition to a Glacier class, while this rule expires the logs instead of moving them.

options.text: The logs are copied into a second bucket and billed twice
options.why: Lifecycle actions work within the same bucket and never make a second billed copy of the logs.

options.text: The logs are kept in one Availability Zone with no spare copy
options.why: An expiration action deletes objects rather than changing where or how they are stored.

incidents.title: The flooded back office
incidents.brief: A burst pipe flooded the cafe's back office overnight. The ordering servers, the inventory server and the drive used for weekly backups all sat under the water. The owner wants a plan that makes the next flood far less painful.

steps.takeaway: Elastic Disaster Recovery replaces a standby data center with low-cost storage, minimal compute and pay-per-use pricing.

read.text: No secondary data center: low-cost storage, minimal compute and pay-per-use pricing.

steps.stem: To protect the ordering servers, the owner first thinks about renting a second back office across town to hold standby servers. Why would AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery cost the cafe less than that plan?

options.text: Replicas sit on storage with minimal compute
options.why: Replicas wait on low-cost storage with minimal compute until a recovery, so the cafe pays for no standby site or idle servers.

options.text: Agents copy block-level changes to AWS nonstop
options.why: This is true of the service, but nonstop copying is how it keeps replicas current, not what makes it cheaper than a second office.

options.text: Recovery drills leave the live servers untouched
options.why: This is true of the service, but safe drills protect the morning orders rather than cutting the cost of standby servers.

options.text: Servers can be restored as of an earlier moment
options.why: This is true of the service, but point-in-time recovery limits data loss and does nothing to lower the cost of standby servers.

steps.takeaway: Tape Gateway lets existing backup software write virtual tapes that AWS keeps in Amazon S3.

read.text: Tape Gateway: virtual tapes in Amazon S3 that backup software treats as tape hardware, with rarely used data movable to a cheaper class.

steps.stem: The cafe replaces its flooded tape drive with Tape Gateway and keeps the same backup software. Where are the virtual tapes that the software writes kept?

options.text: In Amazon S3
options.why: Tape Gateway stores its virtual tapes in Amazon S3, safely away from the cafe's back office.

options.text: On Amazon EBS volumes
options.why: EBS snapshots back up Volume Gateway in stored mode, while virtual tapes are kept somewhere else.

options.text: In an Amazon EFS file system
options.why: EFS is a shared Linux file system for running workloads, not the store behind virtual tapes.

options.text: On the gateway's local disk only
options.why: Keeping tapes only on site would leave them exposed to the next flood, and Tape Gateway puts them in AWS.

steps.takeaway: An app on iSCSI volumes that needs all its data on site plus a cloud copy fits Volume Gateway in stored mode.

read.text: Stored volume mode keeps everything local and backs it up asynchronously as EBS snapshots.

steps.stem: The rebuilt inventory server mounts its storage as iSCSI volumes, and its app needs every piece of data on site for fast reads. The owner also wants a copy in AWS in case of another flood. Which option fits?

options.text: Volume Gateway in stored volume mode
options.why: Stored mode keeps all of the data local and backs it up to AWS as EBS snapshots, matching both needs.

options.text: Volume Gateway in cached volume mode
options.why: Cached mode keeps the main dataset in AWS and only hot data on site, so not every piece of data stays local.

options.text: Amazon S3 File Gateway with a local cache
options.why: It offers an NFS or SMB file share rather than the iSCSI block volumes this server mounts.

options.text: Tape Gateway
options.why: It serves tape backup software for archiving and gives the app no mounted volume for daily reads.

incidents.title: Video files go missing in the training kitchen
incidents.brief: The cafe's new training kitchen films recipe videos, and a small fleet of Linux EC2 instances edits them. Editors complain that a file saved on one instance never shows up on the others, and the manager wants it sorted before the next course starts.

steps.takeaway: Instance store is attached to one instance's host, so its files cannot be shared with other instances.

read.text: It serves one instance only and cannot be shared the way Amazon EFS can.

steps.stem: Each editing instance saves its work to its own EC2 instance store. Why can't the other instances open those files?

options.text: Instance store serves only the instance on its host
options.why: Instance store is disk attached to one instance's host, so no other instance can reach the files on it.

options.text: Instance store is erased whenever its instance stops
options.why: This is true, but the editing instances are running, so it does not explain why the others cannot open the files now.

options.text: Instance store comes free with many instance types
options.why: This is true, but the price of the disk has nothing to do with which instances can reach the files on it.

options.text: Instance store gives very low latency and high I/O
options.why: This is true, but speed on the host does not decide whether another instance can open the files.

steps.takeaway: Files used all day that must survive a zone failure belong in EFS Standard, which spans Availability Zones.

read.text: EFS Standard and Standard-IA: Multi-AZ, with top durability and availability, at a higher price.

steps.stem: The cafe moves the video files to Amazon EFS, and the editing instances are spread across Availability Zones. Editors open the files all day, and the manager wants them reachable even if one zone fails. Which EFS storage class fits?

options.text: EFS Standard
options.why: It replicates files across Availability Zones and suits files opened all day, so one zone failing does not cut access.

options.text: EFS One Zone
options.why: It keeps files in a single Availability Zone, so losing that zone could cut the editors off.

options.text: EFS One Zone-IA
options.why: It sits in a single zone and is priced for rare reads, which fails both of the manager's needs.

options.text: EFS Archive
options.why: It is meant for cold data read a few times a year or less, not files edited every day.

steps.takeaway: EFS lifecycle management can return files to Standard when they are read, but only once the optional rule is turned on.

read.text: An optional rule returns files to Standard when read in IA or Archive, but by default they stay put.

steps.stem: Under the default lifecycle policy, last year's recipe videos have moved out of EFS Standard into cheaper classes. The kitchen now reuses some of them, and the manager wants any video that someone opens to sit in EFS Standard again. What should the cafe do?

options.text: Add the rule that acts on a file's first access
options.why: This optional rule returns a file to Standard once it is read in IA or Archive, which is what the manager wants.

options.text: Leave the default policy, which does this already
options.why: By default a file read in IA or Archive stays where it is, so the default policy alone will not move it back.

options.text: Shorten the idle period before files move to IA
options.why: A shorter idle period only moves files out of Standard sooner and never brings an opened one back.

options.text: Switch the file system to an EFS One Zone class
options.why: One Zone classes change how resilient and cheap storage is, not whether opened files return to Standard.
